title: Topological and metric continuity
terms: continuous map; inverse image criterion; continuity at a point; epsilon-delta continuity; uniform continuity; sequential criterion for continuity.

exposition.text:
A map f : X → Y is continuous when inverse images of open sets are open, equivalently inverse
images of closed sets are closed. It suffices to check a basis for the target topology. Continuity
at x means every neighborhood of f(x) contains the image of some neighborhood of x.
In metric spaces this becomes: for every ε > 0 there is δ > 0 such that d (x, x ) < δ implies

d (f(x), f(x )) < ε. At a single point the preimage of each target neighborhood need only
Y 0
be a neighborhood of that point, not an open set everywhere; the stronger global assertion
characterizes continuity throughout the domain.
A map between metric spaces is uniformly continuous if for every ε > 0 one δ > 0 works for all
pairs x, y: d (x, y) < δ implies d (f(x), f(y)) < ε. Ordinary pointwise continuity allows δ to
X Y
depend on the base point. Sequential continuity is equivalent to continuity for metric spaces:
x → x must imply f(x ) → f(x).

question.text:
Let X = {a, b, c} with topology {∅, {a}, {a, b}, X}. How many continuous maps from X to the
discrete space {0, 1} exist?
(A) 2 (B) 3 (C) 4 (D) 6 (E) 8

solution.text:
The two fibers must both be open, so the fiber of 0 must be clopen. Only ∅ and X are
clopen in this topology. Thus exactly the two constant maps work.

question.text:
Let T be the usual topology on R and L the lower-limit topology. Which maps are continuous:
f : (R, L) → (R, T ), f (x) = x, and g : (R, L) → (R, L), g(x) = −x?
(A) Both.
(B) f only.
(C) g only.
(D) Neither.
(E) Both only on bounded intervals.

solution.text:
−1
The identity from a finer topology to a coarser one is continuous. But g ([0, 1)) = (−1, 0],
which is not lower-limit open at 0 because every basic neighborhood of 0 contains positive
points.

question.text:
Define f(x) = x for rational x and f(x) = −x for irrational x. Let U = (−1, 2). Which
statement is correct?
−1
(A) f is discontinuous at zero because f (U) is not open.
−1
(B) f is continuous at zero, although f (U) is not open in R.
(C) f is continuous everywhere.
−1
(D) f (U) does not contain a neighborhood of zero.
−1
(E) f (U) = (−1, 2)

solution.text:
At zero, |f(x) − f (0)| = |x|, so δ = ε proves continuity. The inverse image of U contains
(−1, 1), hence is a neighborhood of zero. But 3/2 belongs to it and arbitrarily close irra-
tional points greater than one do not, so that inverse image is not open. Continuity at one
point requires a neighborhood there, not global openness of every such preimage.

question.text:
A function between metric spaces is continuous if and only if it
(A) Maps bounded sets to bounded sets
(B) Is uniformly continuous
(C) Maps open sets to open sets
(D) Preserves limits of convergent sequences
(E) Maps closed sets to closed sets

solution.text:
Metric spaces admit the sequential criterion for continuity. Failure of continuity at a point
yields points approaching it whose images stay a fixed positive distance from its image,
proving the converse as well.
